Full text

Abstract

The Trail Making Test (TMT) is among the most widely used neuropsychological tests, and its completion times slow with age. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR) preserves the sequencing structure of the test but replaces pen movements with head-gaze selection in an immersive environment. However, the convergent validity and sensitivity to age of its English-language version in older adults are unknown. Forty-seven younger (20-38 years) and 44 older adults (64-81 years) completed the paper-and-pencil TMT and the TMT-VR in counterbalanced order. Nine scores were derived per format from Parts A and B: completion times, errors, error-adjusted times, and B-A difference scores. Part A and Part B completion times and error-adjusted times of the two formats correlated significantly in the whole sample, and Part B completion times did so within each age group, whereas errors did not. Older adults performed more poorly than younger adults on completion times in both formats, and the age groups were thus differentiated by both the paper-and-pencil TMT and the TMT-VR. The TMT-VR differentiated the age groups statistically better than the paper-and-pencil TMT on Part B completion times, error-adjusted times and errors, but both formats performed comparably on Part A scores. No paper-and-pencil score distinguished between the groups better than its TMT-VR counterpart. The TMT-VR is therefore a valid immersive adaptation of the TMT, and its advantage in age sensitivity lies in the Part B scores. Future studies should aim for clinical validation in older adults.

1. Introduction

The Trail Making Test (TMT; Bowie & Harvey, 2006; Reitan, 1955 Reitan, , 1958) ) requires participants to connect numbered circles in ascending order in Part A (e.g., 1, 2, 3. . .) and alternating numbers and letters to be connected in numerical and alphabetical order in Part B (e.g., 1, A, 2, B, 3. . .). Participants are required to do these tasks as quickly and accurately as possible, without lifting their pencil from the paper. The time taken to complete each part is recorded along with the number of errors made. While the TMT is typically and widely used to assess executive dysfunction (Delis et al., 2001; Lezak, 1995; Reitan & Wolfson, 1993), administering both Parts A and B allows the clinician or researcher to assess visual search, sequencing, psychomotor speed, working memory and task switching in one test (Arbuthnott & Frank, 2000; MacPherson et al., 2019; Sánchez-Cubillo et al., 2009). Part A depends mainly on visuoperceptual abilities and motor speed, whereas Part B additionally loads on working memory and task switching (Arbuthnott & Frank, 2000; Sánchez-Cubillo et al., 2009). The B-A difference score is used to isolate the switching component from speed (Arbuthnott & Frank, 2000; Oosterman et al., 2010; Sánchez-Cubillo et al., 2009).

TMT performance consistently slows with age (Kennedy, 1981; Rasmusson et al., 1998; Tombaugh, 2004). This slowing overlaps substantially with agerelated declines in processing speed and fluid abilities (MacPherson et al., 2019; Salthouse, 1996 Salthouse, , 2011)), and with declining switching and other executive components (Fisk & Sharp, 2004; Idowu & Szameitat, 2023). However, errors are less consistently reported and increase mainly with cognitive impairment (Ashendorf et al., 2008). Moreover, the findings for derived scores are also mixed. For example, while some studies have reported age differences on B-A difference scores and B/A ratio scores (e.g., Drane et al., 2002; Periáñez et al., 2007), others have found age effects on B-A but not B/A ratio scores (e.g., Hester et al., 2005). The brain regions associated with impaired TMT performance also remain debated. Some studies suggest that poor performance, at least in terms of errors, indicates frontal lobe damage (Kopp et al., 2015; Stuss et al., 2001), whereas others suggest that it indicates more global brain changes (Chan et al., 2015; MacPherson et al., 2017). This paper asks whether the scores of an immersive adaptation of the test, the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR; Giatzoglou et al., 2024), correspond with those of the paper-and-pencil TMT and retain its sensitivity to age.

Immersive virtual reality (VR) allows neuropsychological tasks to be presented under experimental control in naturalistic settings (Bohil et al., 2011; Parsons, 2015), with automated administration and scoring. Immersive VR technology has potential benefits for clinical neuropsychology through its ability to mimic real-world scenarios (Clay et al., 2020; De Simone et al., 2023; Hu & Roberts, 2020; Kourtesis et al., 2020) and it has been argued that clinical neuropsychological assessment should reflect advances in technology, psychometrics and neuroscience (Bigler et al., 2025; Bilder & Reise, 2019). The case for ecologically valid measures of executive function (Burgess et al., 2006; Spooner & Pachana, 2006) has motivated function-led virtual environments (Parsons et al., 2017) and technology-based adaptations of established tests (Diaz-Orueta et al., 2020).

VR assessments may also reflect everyday demands that cannot be assessed in the clinic, such as navigating crowded streets or avoiding unexpected obstacles (Kourtesis et al., 2020; Parsons, 2015). VR testing is moving from hand-held controllers to hands-free inputs that better reflect natural behaviour and reduce motor load (González-Erena et al., 2025). An adaptation nevertheless changes the demands of the test. A pen movement may become head, gaze or controller selection, and the display, feedback and layout change. Therefore, the joint position paper of the American Academy of Clinical Neuropsychology and the National Academy of Neuropsychology treats a computerised adaptation as a new instrument whose psychometric properties must be demonstrated before clinical use (Bauer et al., 2012). Because the properties of the paper-and-pencil TMT are well established, an adaptation can be evaluated against them. Convergent validity (i.e., the correspondence between the scores of the adaptation and those of the established test) has been shown for a computerised TMT. Its completion times correlated strongly with paper-and-pencil completion times and discriminated between younger and older adults (Park & Schott, 2022). Immersive versions of the Color Trails Test, a variant of the TMT, have likewise shown convergent validity (Plotnik et al., 2017 (Plotnik et al., , 2021)), albeit with targets selected by a hand-held pointing device and with added measures of cognitivemotor interaction. They have also shown age effects (Ben Gal et al., 2019; Plotnik et al., 2017 Plotnik et al., , 2021)), as the paper-and-pencil TMT reliably does on completion times (Kennedy, 1981; Tombaugh, 2004). Therefore, the age-group comparison provides a second criterion on which any adaptation should be assessed. Replacing the pen with head movement responses may reproduce this correspondence and these age effects, attenuate them or amplify them, because age may affect head-movement responses differently from pen movements. This is an empirical question for any TMT adaptation and its scores.

The TMT-VR preserves the sequencing structure of the TMT but replaces pen movements with other ways of selecting targets in an immersive environment (Giatzoglou et al., 2024; Kourtesis et al., 2025). Across young and middle adulthood, head-gaze selection was found to be the fastest mode on Part B with the fewest selection errors. Head-gaze selection needs neither eye-tracking calibration, which can fail with progressive lenses or in poor lighting, nor a hand-held controller, and is therefore the mode open to the widest range of participants, including older adults (Kourtesis et al., 2025). In Greek-speaking young adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and neurotypical controls, scores on the Greek version of the TMT-VR correlated with those of the Greek paperand-pencil TMT (Gounari et al., 2025). Furthermore, Part B completion times for the Greek version correlated moderately with paper-and-pencil times in healthy older adults and more weakly in those with mild cognitive impairment (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou, et al., 2026). In the same study, the TMT-VR Part B completion times and wrong-target errors distinguished the two groups. In a lifespan sample of 230 Greek-speaking adults aged 19-90 years, older age was strongly associated with longer completion times and moderately with more wrong-target errors with head-gaze selection (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou, Anastasopoulou, et al., 2026). However, the English-language version, which presents its instructions in English and the letters of the English alphabet in Part B, has not been examined for convergent validity or sensitivity to age in older adults. It is also unknown whether the TMT-VR distinguishes younger from older adults as well as the paper-and-pencil test does. The usability, acceptability and tolerability of the Englishlanguage version in the present sample of younger and older adults have already been demonstrated in Kourtesis, O'Connor, and MacPherson (2026b).

The present study compared the TMT-VR with headgaze selection and the paper-and-pencil TMT in 47 younger adults aged 20-38 years and 44 older adults aged 64-81 years. It had two aims. The first was to establish the convergent validity of the TMT-VR, that is, whether its completion times, errors and error-adjusted scores were correlated with the corresponding paperand-pencil scores, in the whole sample and within each age group. The second was to examine whether the age differences reported for the paper-and-pencil TMT were also found for the TMT-VR, and whether either format distinguished between the age groups better. Completion times were expected to correspond across formats, as in previous digital and immersive adaptations (Gounari et al., 2025; Park & Schott, 2022; Plotnik et al., 2021). Given the age effects found with the Greek version (Kour-tesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou, Anastasopoulou, et al., 2026), the TMT-VR was expected to distinguish between the age groups at least as well as the paper-and-pencil test.

2. Method

>Method

2.1. Participants

The sample comprised 91 adults with 5-22 years of education (M = 16.40, SD = 2.86): 47 younger adults aged 20-38 years (M = 25.1, SD = 4.1; 25 women) with 16.64 years of education (SD = 3.00, range = 5-22) and 44 older adults aged 64-81 years (M = 71.8, SD = 4.9; 24 women) with 16.14 years of education (SD = 2.71, range = 10-21). The age groups did not differ significantly in sex composition (Fisher's exact test, p = 1.000) or education (Welch's t-test, p = .404). Seventy-one participants were tested at the University of Edinburgh. They were recruited through the volunteer panel of the School of Philosophy, Psychology and Language Sciences, postgraduate mailing lists, word of mouth and posters, and received £20 for their participation. Twenty participants (10 younger and 10 older adults), all native English speakers, were tested at The American College of Greece (ACG) under the identical protocol. They were recruited through the ACG volunteer panel and the Open Care Centre for the Elderly (KAPI) of Aghia Paraskevi, and received no payment. No one had a history of neurological or psychiatric conditions, learning difficulties, or conditions affecting balance. They also did not have serious susceptibility to motion sickness, defined by a Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire-Short (MSSQ-Short; Golding, 2006) total score above 30 (observed maximum = 29.5). Nor were they at risk of falls, which was assessed by asking them to cross their arms and stand on one leg for three seconds (Giorgetti et al., 1998). All participants provided written informed consent. The study was approved by the PPLS Research Ethics Committee of the University of Edinburgh (No. 244-2324/13) and the Institutional Review Board of The American College of Greece (No. 202602564). It was also approved by the Research Ethics and Deontology Committee (E.H.Δ.E.) of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens (protocol No. 20579/5.3.2024, decision No. 152/4.4.2024), and it was performed in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki. No participant withdrew or was excluded after screening, and all 91 records were complete for the analysed variables.

The sample size was planned a priori to detect moderate to large effects (Cohen, 1988). With two-sided 𝛼 = .05 and 80% power, a moderate correlation between the two formats (r = .30) requires 84 participants in the whole sample, and a moderate-to-large difference between the age groups (d = 0.74) requires 30 participants per group. The final sample of 91 participants, 47 younger and 44 older adults, exceeded both requirements.

2.2. Apparatus and TMT-VR

The English-language version of the TMT-VR (build TMT-VR_2025, version 0.1, 19 May 2025; Unity 2021.3.0f1, Windows 64-bit, OpenXR with the SteamVR runtime) was presented on an HTC VIVE Pro Eye headmounted display (HTC Corporation, Taoyuan, Taiwan; 1440 × 1600 pixels per eye, 90 Hz, 110° field of view). The headset was tracked by two SteamVR base stations and driven by a laptop with an Intel Core i7-8750H processor, 16 GB of RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2070 Max-Q graphics processor. Targets were selected by head gaze. A ray cast from the headset positioned a central reticle, and a target was registered when the reticle had rested on it for 0.5 s, the dwell threshold set on every target in the build. Selection therefore used head orientation rather than eye tracking and required no hand-held controller. Participants stood throughout the assessment, with the experimenter beside them.

Each part of the TMT-VR presented numbered or numbered and lettered blocks at randomly generated positions in a plain virtual room (see Figure 1). The 25 positions were drawn from a pool of 168 candidate positions. Part A required the numbers 1 to 25 to be selected in ascending order, and Part B required alternation between numbers and the letters of the English alphabet (1-A-2-B . . .). A short tone marked the arrival of the reticle on a block, and a confirmation tone indicated a correct selection where the block turned yellow and a yellow trail was drawn from the previous block. An incorrect selection was indicated by a buzzer and turned the block briefly red, after which the participant went back to the last correct target. The feedback sounds were spatialised at the position of the block. The TMT-VR program recorded the completion times and the number of errors (i.e., wrong-target selections) for each part.

2.3. Paper-and-Pencil TMT

The conventional paper-and-pencil TMT (Bowie & Harvey, 2006; Reitan, 1958) was administered by the experimenter in its standard form. In Part A, participants drew a continuous line connecting 25 numbered circles in ascending order. In Part B, they connected 25 numbered and lettered circles in alternating numerical and alphabetical order. Both parts were completed as quickly as possible and without lifting the pencil from the paper. Errors were pointed out as they occurred and corrected without stopping the clock. The completion times for each part and the number of errors were recorded.

2.4. Procedure

Participants first provided demographic information and completed questionnaires on gaming experience (Gaming Skills Questionnaire; Lepida et al., 2025; Zioga et al., 2024) and technology experience, and the MSSQ-Short. The order of the paper-and-pencil TMT and the TMT-VR was counterbalanced across participants to avoid practice effects (Buck et al., 2008). Before the TMT-VR, the experimenter explained head-controlled selection, the required sequences and the importance of both speed and accuracy. Participants were also warned that blocks could obscure one another, so that they might need to turn to locate a target. Narrated in-environment videos in English provided the instructions, and a practice trial preceded each part (see Figure 1). The TMT-VR took approximately 10-15 min to administer. No participant required assistance beyond this briefing, and no session was interrupted or stopped. After the TMT-VR, participants completed questionnaires on cybersickness, usability, user experience and acceptability (Kourtesis, O'Connor, & MacPherson, 2026b).

2.5. Performance Scores

Nine scores were derived from the completion times and errors for each format, following the score definitions of the TMT-VR lifespan study (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou, Anastasopoulou, et al., 2026)

2.6. Statistical Analyses

All analyses were conducted in R 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024) with the packages 'sandwich' (Zeileis et al., 2020) and 'pROC' (Robin et al., 2011), except the sample comparisons of Table 1, which were computed in Python 3.13 with SciPy 1.18 (Virtanen et al., 2020). Tests were two-sided with 𝛼 = .05, confidence intervals (CIs) were pointwise 95% intervals, and bootstrap CIs used 5,000 paired-participant resamples. To correct for multiple comparisons, p values were Holm-adjusted (Holm, 1979) within families of related tests (e.g., the nine TMT-VR scores). The nine-score families were defined after the analysis had been archived, when the B/A ratio, the two TMT-VR selection-distance scores and the three total scores were removed to keep the results succinct. The completion times, errors and B-A differences retained are those most often reported in TMT studies. The Supporting Information reports the results under both definitions of the families.

The age groups were compared on technology experience and motion sickness susceptibility with Welch's t-tests. Gaming experience was compared with the Mann-Whitney U test as its scores were positively skewed. Holm adjustment was applied across the three tests.

Convergent validity was examined through the correlations between the corresponding paper-and-pencil and TMT-VR scores, for the whole sample and within each age group, with Fisher-z and bootstrap CIs. Pearson correlations were used for the completion-time scores (Part A, Part B, B-A and the three error-adjusted times) and Spearman correlations for the three error scores. The equivalent coefficients were also computed as sensitivity analyses (Supporting Information, Section S4). When an error score had zero variance in a bootstrap resample, the correlation could not be computed, and that resample was counted as not estimable. Holm adjustment was applied across the nine pairs within the whole sample and then applied separately within each age group.

The age effects were examined for every score in both formats using three statistics. The first was the olderminus-younger difference with Welch's t-test and CI. The second was Hedges' g with a bootstrap CI. The third was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC; i.e., the probability that a randomly chosen older participant obtained the poorer score) with a DeLong CI (DeLong et al., 1988). The Welch tests were Holmadjusted within each format (i.e., VR or paper-and-pencil). The two formats were then compared on each of the corresponding scores with paired DeLong tests of the VR-minus-paper AUC difference, Holm-adjusted across the nine pairs, and with paired bootstrap CIs of the difference in g. The correlations of the scores with age and education within each age group were supplementary analyses and are reported in Section S6 of the Supporting Information.

De-identified participant-level data (Kourtesis, O'Connor, & MacPherson, 2026a), variable definitions, analysis scripts and archived numerical outputs are openly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23270971. The accompanying README describes the included materials and reproduction limitations. The Supporting Information reports every analysis in full, including the sensitivity analyses.

3. Results

>Results

3.1. Sample Characteristics

Table 1 presents the gaming experience, technology experience and motion sickness susceptibility of the two age groups. The groups did not differ significantly in motion sickness susceptibility (Holm p = .903). However, younger participants reported significantly more gaming and technology experience than older participants (both Holm p < .001). Reported VR use was minimal, with 89 of the 91 participants giving the lowest VR frequency rating.

3.2. Convergent Validity

Table 2 presents the correlations between the corresponding paper-and-pencil and TMT-VR scores. Figure 2 The sensitivity analyses led to the same conclusions. With Spearman coefficients, every completion-time score still corresponded across formats, and with Pearson coefficients, the errors still did not, except for one weak association for the B-A error differences in the whole sample whose bootstrap interval included zero. The sensitivity analyses with the alternative coefficients are reported in Section S4 of the Supporting Information.

3.3. Age Group by TMT Format

Table 3 presents the performance scores of the two age groups for the TMT-VR and paper-and-pencil TMT, and Table 4 presents the statistics examining the age effects in each format. In terms of the AUC analysis, the TMT-VR Part A and Part B completion times and error-adjusted times distinguished the two age groups well, and Part B errors did so modestly. However, Part A errors did not distinguish the two age groups. Of the equivalent paper-and-pencil TMT measures, the Part A completion and error-adjusted times also distinguished the groups well, but the Part B times showed only modest discrimination and the errors none. The B-A scores showed weak or no discrimination in either format. In the Welch tests for the paper-and-pencil TMT, older adults were significantly slower on the Part A completion and error-adjusted times (both Holm p < .001) and on Part B completion times (Holm p = .046). However, the age difference in paper-and-pencil Part B completion times was not significant when the Holm adjustment covered all 13 paper-and-pencil scores of the archived analysis (Holm p = .059). Part B error-adjusted times (Holm p = .104) and the errors and B-A scores (all Holm p = 1.000) did not differ significantly between the age groups. In the TMT-VR, only Part A errors and the B-A scores did not differ significantly between the age groups (all Holm p ≥ .070). Older adults were significantly slower than younger adults on the TMT-VR Part A and Part B completion times and error-adjusted times, and made significantly more Part B errors (all Holm p ≤ .004).

ΔAUC denotes the difference between the AUCs for the two formats for the same score, that is, the TMT-VR AUC minus the paper-and-pencil AUC (Table 4). A positive ΔAUC therefore means that the TMT-VR distinguished between the age groups better than the paper-and-pencil test. The TMT-VR differentiated the age groups statistically better than the paper-and-pencil test on Part B completion times, Part B error-adjusted times and Part B errors (all Holm p ≤ .014). However, for the Part A and B-A scores, the formats did not differ significantly in their ability to differentiate between the two age groups (all Holm p ≥ .261). The paired difference in g between the formats favoured the TMT-VR on the B-A error difference, albeit with an interval not corrected for multiple comparisons, while the AUC comparison did not (Supporting Information, Section S5). On every Table 2. TMT = Trail Making Test; TMT-VR = Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality.

other score, the paired differences in g agreed with the AUC comparison, favouring the TMT-VR on the three Part B scores. The complete within-group age and education correlations are reported in Section S6 of the Supporting Information.

4. Discussion

This study examined the convergent validity of the TMT-VR against the traditional paper-and-pencil TMT and whether age effects exist for both formats. Two findings emerged. First, the completion times and erroradjusted times corresponded across formats in the whole sample, and Part B completion times did so within each age group, whereas the errors did not. Second, within each format, the Welch tests, Hedges' g and the AUCs showed that both formats (i.e., VR and paper-and-pencil) differentiated the two age groups on completion times. Between the formats, the paired comparison of the AUCs showed that the TMT-VR did so better on Part B completion times, error-adjusted times and errors. On Part A, the two formats did not differ in how well they distinguished between the groups on completion times and error-adjusted times, and neither format distinguished them on Part A errors. No paper-and-pencil score distinguished between the age groups better than its TMT-VR counterpart.

4.1. Convergent Validity

Paper-and-pencil and TMT-VR completion times were significantly correlated with one another. The Part B completion times for the two formats (i.e., TMT-VR and paper-and-pencil) were also correlated within each age group, and the Part B error-adjusted times within the older group. Our Part A and Part B correlations were a little lower than those reported between the paperand-pencil Color Trails Test and its immersive versions (Plotnik et al., 2021), but those versions used a handheld pointer. Our correlations are also consistent with the strong correspondence between the paper-and-pencil and computerised TMT durations (Park & Schott, 2022). These findings extend the convergent-validity evidence for the TMT-VR from the Greek version (Gounari et al., 2025; Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou, et al., 2026) to the Englishlanguage version in younger and older adults. They also show that participants who were slower on the paper-andpencil test tended to be slower on the TMT-VR, despite the change from pen to head movement. Within our older group, the Part A and Part B correspondences were close to those of the Greek version in healthy older adults (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou, et al., 2026). In both studies, the Part B correspondence remained significant after correction, whereas the Part A correspondence did not. This agreement suggests a similar correspondence with the paper-and-pencil test in the two language versions, albeit across studies that also differed in headset, posture and sample.

In the whole sample, the B-A differences correlated less strongly across formats than the Part A and Part B times, possibly for two reasons. First, the difference score is meant to isolate switching. On paper, however, the layout of Part B also demands more visual search and pen movement than that of Part A (Gaudino et al., 1995). In the TMT-VR, both parts draw their positions at random from the same pool, so the two B-A scores mix switching with different layout demands. Second, subtracting Part A removes the general speed that the two formats share, which is what makes their completion times correlate. The weaker Part A correspondence within the younger group more plausibly reflects the narrow range of Part A times among fast young adults than the change of format. With about 45 participants per age group, only strong correlations could be detected reliably within a group, so a weaker correspondence between the Part A scores of the two formats may have gone undetected. Larger age groups are needed to resolve this.

Errors, in contrast, did not correspond between the TMT-VR and paper-and-pencil formats. However, most participants did not make errors on the paper-and-pencil TMT, which is consistent with the low error rates found in healthy older adults performing the conventional test (Ashendorf et al., 2008). Wrong-target selections in the TMT-VR were also uncommon. Therefore, a correlation between errors cannot be estimated reliably with such low variability. Completion times, by contrast, varied across all participants, so the completion-time and erroradjusted scores carry the convergent evidence for the TMT-VR.

4.2. Sensitivity to Age

Both TMT formats showed age differences on completion times, as is consistently reported in studies using the paper-and-pencil TMT (Kennedy, 1981; Tombaugh, 2004). Our AUC analysis demonstrated that the TMT-VR distinguished between younger and older adults more effectively on the Part B completion times, error-adjusted times and errors than the paper-and-pencil TMT. Three potential properties of the immersive format may account for this. The first is the response demand. Both formats engage psychomotor control, which declines with age (Hoogendam et al., 2014). The paper-and-pencil TMT is a familiar eye-hand coordination task, in which the pen is guided from circle to circle on a page. Head-gaze selection has no hand component. The target is selected by turning the head and holding one's gaze on it, as people do when they search their surroundings, albeit here against the clock and with a brief hold on each target. In a VR pointing task, the slowing of older adults relative to younger adults was larger with some selection techniques than with others (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou, Roussos, & Roussou, 2026). The age sensitivity of an immersive score may therefore depend partly on how the target is selected. The second is the visual-search demand. While both formats required visual search (Crowe, 1998), in the TMT-VR, the targets occupy randomised positions in a three-dimensional space that extend beyond the field of view, so locating the next target requires head-driven search rather than glancing across a page. Search slows with age, particularly when the display is cluttered and the target must be located among distractors (Hommel et al., 2004; Madden, 2007; Plude & Doussard-Roosevelt, 1989). Searching the space around oneself for the next target, among blocks that can hide one another, may also resemble everyday search more closely than scanning a page does (Kourtesis et al., 2020; Parsons, 2015).

The third property is the scale of the scores. TMT-VR completion times were two to three times as long as the paper-and-pencil TMT ones, as in Plotnik et al. (2021), whose immersive versions also took longer than the paper test. The older group was also more variable in their completion times on the TMT-VR. Individual differences therefore may have more room to express themselves than in the briefer paper-and-pencil test. In contrast, on Part A, the two formats did not differ significantly in distinguishing the age groups. The advantage of the TMT-VR appears to be on Part B. This is in line with the lifespan study of the Greek version in 230 adults, in which completion times, error-adjusted times and wrong-target errors were the TMT-VR scores most sensitive to age (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou, Anastasopoulou, et al., 2026). Two practical features follow from these results. The TMT-VR records the completion times and every wrong-target selection automatically, and its Part B scores distinguished the age groups better than the paper-and-pencil scores did. For the clinician, the TMT-VR therefore offers an automated Part B measure that is more sensitive to age. The B-A difference scores did not identify age differences in either format. The literature on the derived scores is mixed: some studies found age differences on both the B-A and the B/A scores (Drane et al., 2002; Periáñez et al., 2007), whereas Hester et al. (2005) found them on B-A but not B/A. Our null result for B-A is consistent with Salthouse (2011), who found that age differences in trail-making performance overlap almost completely with individual differences in speed and fluid abilities. The B-A score retains the switching component, but in our healthy participants, the switching cost did not add significantly to the age difference already present in Part A. The error-adjusted times, by contrast, differentiated the two age groups about as well as the raw completion times. The reason is that the two scores carry nearly the same information. In both formats, the time incorporates errors because the participant has to return to the last correct target before continuing.

It should be noted that the age sensitivity shown here is a prerequisite for clinical use, not evidence of clinical validity. Our study examines the TMT-VR's ability to distinguish performance between healthy younger and older adults and not clinically diagnosed cognitive impairment.

In older adults with and without mild cognitive impairment, the Part B completion times of the Greek TMT-VR version and the paper-and-pencil test distinguished the two groups, with no detectable difference between the formats (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou, et al., 2026). In that study, TMT-VR Part B and B-A error scores distinguished the groups more strongly than the paper-and-pencil errors, albeit without a format difference that remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In both versions, the Part B wrong-target errors of the TMT-VR distinguished the groups, whereas the paper-and-pencil errors did so weakly or not at all. Therefore, future work in larger clinical samples is required to determine whether the sensitivity of the English-language version translates into the detection of clinical conditions, such as mild cognitive impairment.

4.3. Implications

For the clinical neuropsychologist, the current results support three conclusions. First, the completion times and error-adjusted scores of the TMT-VR are related to those measured using the paper-and-pencil TMT; therefore, the immersive adaptation retains what the original test measures. These correlations show that the TMT-VR and paper-and-pencil scores are associated but not the same. Second, the Part B completion times, error-adjusted times and wrong-target errors are more sensitive to healthy ageing in the immersive format. The TMT-VR is therefore better at distinguishing older from younger adults on the basis of their performance than the paper-and-pencil test. Finally, as one would expect, the paper-and-pencil normative data do not transfer. TMT-VR completion times are two to three times as long, so age referencing of the TMT-VR has to be built on its own scores, for each language version.

The usability, acceptability and tolerability of the TMT-VR in the same participants have already been found to be favourable in both age groups (Kourtesis, O'Connor, & MacPherson, 2026b). The lack of established psychometric properties of digital versions of tests has likely contributed to the limited adoption of technology by many neuropsychologists (Miller & Barr, 2017). A strength of our study is therefore the examination of the convergent validity of the TMT-VR in relation to the paper-and-pencil version, in the age group for which the test is most often used. Together with the automatic recording of errors and the standardised administration, these properties make the TMT-VR a candidate for clinical evaluation.

4.4. Limitations and Future Studies

The current study has some limitations that should be examined through future research. First, the sample consisted of two age groups of relatively highly educated adults, with no participants in middle adulthood. The results therefore describe the contrast between younger and older adulthood but not how performance changes across the lifespan. Second, the evaluation of the TMT-VR rests on one testing session, so its test-retest reliability and practice effects, which the paper-and-pencil test shows over short intervals (Buck et al., 2008), remain unexamined. Third, the low error rates limited the precision of our error analyses, which is similar to the findings of the paper-and-pencil test in healthy adults (Ashendorf et al., 2008). However, Stuss et al. (2001) claimed that it was TMT errors rather than slow speed that indicated cognitive impairment associated with frontal lobe damage.

Future studies follow from these limitations. Sampling across the adult age range and in more diversely educated individuals is needed before the age sensitivity of the scores can be generalised. A second session would establish test-retest reliability and practice effects. Larger and clinical samples are required to examine whether the wrong-target errors of the English-language version carry diagnostic information. The controller mode of the TMT-VR, which retains the eye-hand coordination that head-gaze selection removes, should also be compared with the head-gaze mode in older adults. Eye-hand coordination is impaired in early Alzheimer's disease and in older adults at increased risk of it (Hawkins & Sergio, 2014; Tippett & Sergio, 2006), so the controller mode may prove more sensitive to age and more informative in clinical groups.

5. Conclusion

The completion times and error-adjusted times of the English-language version of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality, using head-gaze selection, corresponded with those of the paper-and-pencil test, whereas the errors did not. Part B completion times also corresponded within each age group. The TMT-VR distinguished healthy older from younger adults more effectively than the paper-and-pencil test on the Part B completion times, error-adjusted times and errors, but not on Part A. The TMT-VR is therefore a valid immersive adaptation of the TMT, and it brings the search demands of a threedimensional environment into a standardised, automatically scored test (Kourtesis et al., 2020; Parsons, 2015). It is more sensitive to age than the original test on the Part B scores, and it can now proceed to normative referencing by age, sex and education, to intra-individual comparisons over time, and to clinical validation.

Section S1. Data, Scores and Correction Families

The data set comprises 91 participants, 47 younger adults aged 20-38 years and 44 older adults aged 64-81 years, with complete records for every analysed variable. Nothing was imputed, winsorised or excluded. The analysis script verified the checksum of the data workbook before running. Table S1 defines the nine corresponding scores of each format.

Table S1 Definitions of the Nine Corresponding Scores of Each Format The archived analysis also examined the B/A completion-time ratio for each format, the mean selection distance of each TMT-VR part and the total (Part A + Part B) completion times, errors and adjusted times for each format. These scores were removed from the report after the analysis record was archived, and the correction families were redefined over the nine reported scores (Table S2). Every adjusted p value in Sections S4-S6 is given under both definitions.

The original definition is that of the analysis record, which included the B/A completion-time ratio for each format, the Part A and Part B mean selection distances of the TMT-VR and the total scores. A result differs in statistical significance when its Holm-adjusted p value lies on different sides of .05 under the two definitions.

Six results differ in statistical significance between the two definitions, and each is statistically significant after correction under the nine-score definition only. In the age-group comparison, the paper-and-pencil Part B completion times differ between the age groups (Hedges' g = 0.58; Holm p = .046, against .059 under the original definition), which the article discloses. In the older group, TMT-VR Part B completion times (r = .39; Holm p = .044, against .098), Part B error-adjusted times (r = .41; Holm p = .032, against .064) and the B-A error difference (𝜌 = .37; Holm p = .026, against .116) correlate with age. In the whole sample, paper-and-pencil Part B error-adjusted times (r = .27; Holm p = .028, against .076) and the TMT-VR B-A error difference (𝜌 = .27; Holm p = .021, against .073) correlate with age. Every other result is the same under both definitions.

Analysis settings. All analyses were conducted in R 4.4.1 with the packages 'sandwich' 3.1-3 and 'pROC' 1.19.0.1, except the sample comparisons of Table 1 of the article, which were computed in Python 3.13 with SciPy 1.18. Tests were two-sided with 𝛼 = .05, and every interval is a pointwise 95% interval. Bootstrap intervals are percentile intervals from 5,000 resamples (seed 20260921). The correlation intervals resampled participants together with both of their scores. The intervals of Hedges' g resampled participants within each age group, and those of the difference in g between the formats used the same resampled participants for both formats. A resample in which an error score had no variance could not yield a correlation and was counted as not estimable. These counts are the diagnostics of the low number of errors, and they are reported with every interval. The AUC intervals and the paired comparisons of the AUCs used DeLong's method. Fisher-z intervals are also given for the Spearman coefficients, as an approximation.

Section S4. Convergent Validity: Complete Correlation Families

Tables S7-S9 report the correlations between the corresponding paper-and-pencil and TMT-VR scores in the whole sample, the younger group and the older group. Each table gives the primary family presented in the article (Pearson r for the completion-time scores and Spearman 𝜌 for the error scores) and the complete Pearson and Spearman families. Every coefficient has a Fisher-z and a bootstrap interval, and every adjusted p value is given under both family definitions. In the whole sample, every completion-time correspondence was statistically significant after correction in both the Pearson and the Spearman family, so the conclusion of the article does not depend on the correlation method. The Spearman coefficients of the completion-time scores are larger, because the completion-time distributions are right-skewed. Beyond the correspondences supported in the primary family, the Spearman family supported the Part B error-adjusted correspondence in the younger group (𝜌 = .54) and the Part A completion-time, Part A error-adjusted and B-A error-adjusted correspondences in the older group (𝜌 = .47, .48 and .41). The error scores did not correspond in the Spearman family. In the Pearson family, the B-A error difference in the whole sample was statistically significant after correction (r = .27; Holm p = .027), but its bootstrap interval included zero; no other error correspondence was significant.

Section S5. Age-Group Differences: Test Statistics

Table S10 reports the comparison of the age groups on each of the nine scores for each format, with Welch's t-test, the Mann-Whitney test, Hedges' g and the AUC. Table S11 reports the comparison of the formats on each corresponding score. One result depends on the family definition (paper-and-pencil Part B completion times; Section S1). The TMT-VR distinguished between the age groups better than the paper-and-pencil test on Part B completion times, Part B error-adjusted times and Part B errors, and the two formats did not differ significantly on the other six scores.

Supporting Information Validity and Age Sensitivity of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality: A Comparison with the Paper-and-Pencil Test in Younger and Older Adults

Panagiotis Kourtesis, Dante O'Connor, Sarah E. MacPherson This Supporting Information reports in full the analyses summarised in the article. Section S1 defines the scores and the families of tests within which p values were adjusted. Section S2 gives the descriptive statistics of the performance scores, and Section S3 the demographic comparisons. Section S4 reports the complete convergent-validity families, and Section S5 the test statistics of the age-group differences and of the comparison of the formats. Section S6 reports the correlations of the scores with age and with years of education in the whole sample and in each age group. Every value is taken from the archived outputs of the analysis.

Section S6. Correlations of the Scores With Age and Education

Tables S12-S14 report the correlations of the scores with age in the whole sample, the younger group and the older group, and Tables S15-S17 the correlations with years of education. These analyses are supplementary to the age-group comparison of the article. No participant was aged 39-63 years, so the whole-sample age correlations mainly reflect the difference between the age groups. Within the younger group, whose ages spanned across 18 years, no score correlated with age in either format (|r| ≤ .24; no Holm p below .05 under either definition). Within the older group, whose ages spanned across 17 years, TMT-VR Part B errors correlated with age under both definitions (𝜌 = .43, 95% CI [.17, .66]; Holm p = .010, or .046 under the original definition). TMT-VR Part B completion times, Part B error-adjusted times and the B-A error difference scores correlated with age under the nine-score definition only (Section S1). No paper-and-pencil score correlated with age within either group. In the older group, more years of education accompanied fewer TMT-VR Part B errors (𝜌 = -.44, 95% CI [-.67, -.16]; Holm p = .008, or .042 under the original definition). No other association with education was statistically significant after correction.

Figure 1.

Figure 1. Screenshots from the TMT-VR at different stages of Part A and Part B. Top row: Part A video tutorial (left), practice trial (middle) and main test (right). Bottom row: Part B video tutorial (left), practice trial (middle) and main test (right). Targets are selected by resting the central head-gaze reticle on a block; a correct selection turns the block yellow and draws the trail from the previous target. English-language demonstrations: Task A video (https://www.youtube.com/watch? v=npki7i4OnwY) and Task B video (https://www.youtube.com/watch? v=immvIkOyVuA).

. These included Part A and Part B completion times and the B-A completion time difference score. They also included Part A, Part B, and B-A errors, with wrong-target selections as the TMT-VR errors. Error-adjusted scores were also derived for Part A, Part B, and B-A completion times. An error-adjusted time multiplied the completion time by one plus the proportion of the 24 transitions on which an error was made. An error therefore extended the time by the proportion of the sequence it represented. The B/A ratio scores are not reported, as they overlap with the B-A difference scores.

plots the TMT-VR against the paper-and-pencil completion times for Part A and Part B. In the whole sample, every completion-time score corresponded across the two formats (all Holm p ≤ .003). Within the older group, Part B completion times and Part B error-adjusted times corresponded significantly after correction. Within the younger group, Part B completion times corresponded significantly. The Part A correspondence was weaker

Figure 3 shows Hedges' g and the AUC for every score in both formats. Completion times were about three times as long in the TMT-VR as on paper for Part A and about twice as long for Part B, and the older group was more variable as well as slower in both formats. Errors were few in both formats. On paper, 81 participants (89%) made no Part A error and 60 (66%) made no Part B error. In the TMT-VR, 60 participants (66%) made no wrong-target selection on Part A and 49 (54%) made none on Part B.

Figure 2. Association between the paper-and-pencil and TMT-VR completion times. Scatter plots of the TMT-VR against the paper-and-pencil completion times for Part A (a) and Part B (b) in the 91 participants. Filled circles are younger adults (20-38 years, n = 47) and open triangles are older adults (64-81 years, n = 44). The line is the least-squares fit in the whole sample. The value of r is the Pearson correlation in the whole sample, with its 95% bootstrap confidence interval (5,000 resamples), as inTable 2. TMT = Trail Making Test; TMT-VR = Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality.

Figure 3.

Figure 3. Age-group effects on the nine scores of each format. (a) Hedges' g for the older minus the younger group, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Positive values indicate poorer performance in the older group. (b) The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for the discrimination of the older from the younger group, with 95% DeLong confidence intervals. The vertical lines mark no effect (g = 0; AUC = .5, chance). Filled circles are the TMT-VR scores and open squares are the paper-and-pencil scores. ΔAUC is the difference between the two AUCs (the TMT-VR AUC minus the paper-and-pencil AUC), shown for the three scores on which the paired comparison of the AUCs was statistically significant after Holm correction (marked with an asterisk, Holm p < .05; Table 4). B-A = Part B minus Part A; error-adjusted time = completion time × (1 + errors/24); TMT = Trail Making Test; TMT-VR = Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality.
